title: The infodemics of COVID-19 amongst healthcare professionals in India
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 758 Indian healthcare professionals and medical students reporting the share of respondents who say they received COVID-19 misinformation: 517 (68.2%, 95% CI 64.8-71.5), plus a separate Likert item on which 75% agreed or strongly agreed they had received inaccurate information. Both are RECALL (self-reported exposure) shares with an explicit denominator.

estimates.platform: Online questionnaire (Google Forms); the misinformation itself was reported as coming from social media, family and friends, WhatsApp, TV and online news
estimates.measure_type: % of healthcare professionals and medical students who reported having received misinformation about COVID-19
estimates.value_raw: Misinformation received: Yes 517 (68.2%), 95% CI 64.8%-71.5%; No 241 (31.8%), of 758 participants
estimates.denominator: 758 analysed respondents (778 forms received, 20 incomplete): 255 medical students (33.6%), 335 non-specialist doctors (44.2%) and 168 specialists (22.1%), recruited by snowball sampling of Indian healthcare personnel
estimates.definition: Respondents answered yes/no to having received misinformation; the authors gloss the affirmative as having 'identified receiving information they deem to be partially or completely inaccurate'. The judgement of what counted as misinformation was the respondent's own.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to false information which is shared without any intention of causing harm, while disinformation is fake information which has been deliberately created and shared to cause harm. The present study limits itself to misinformation only."
estimates.source_quote: A total of 517 (68.2%) participants accepted receiving misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results; Results, 'Sources of misinformation' (p. 278) and Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report: no external verification of what the respondents classified as misinformation. The authors flag this themselves - 'the interpretation of misinformation by the respondents may not be very accurate especially in the case of medical students'. The questionnaire was developed after a literature search and expert consultation, cognitively pretested on 30 respondents with think-aloud feedback and pilot-tested on a further 50.
estimates.moderator_quote: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among the healthcare personnel in India from 24 Mar 2020 to 10 Apr 2020. The snowballing sampling technique was used for this online survey. ... A total of 778 forms were received, out of which 20 forms were incomplete, and hence, data of 758 participants were analysed.
estimates.notes: 517/758 = 68.2%, matching the verbatim value and the reported 95% CI; the Discussion prints the same figure as 68.12%. No recall WINDOW is specified for this item (it asks about receiving misinformation, not about the last week/month), so the reference period is effectively the pandemic up to the survey date. Respondent-judged, hence breadth=misleading ('partially or completely inaccurate') and ground_truth=self_report. Population is professional (doctors and medical students), not the general public; the sample is a self-selected snowball of internet-using literate healthcare workers, which the authors concede limits generalisability.

estimates.measure_type: % of the same respondents who agreed or strongly agreed on a Likert item that they had received inaccurate information about COVID-19
estimates.value_raw: 75% of all respondents either agree or strongly agree about ... inaccurate information
estimates.definition: Agreement (agree or strongly agree, on the five-point Likert battery shown in Fig 4) with a statement about having received inaccurate information about COVID-19.
estimates.misinfo_def: As above; the study limits itself to misinformation (false information shared without intent to harm).
estimates.source_quote: but more than that 75% agreed to having received inaccurate information.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report on a five-point agreement scale; no external verification.
estimates.moderator_quote: Questions about the infodemics of COVID-19 were part of the survey instrument. The responses gathered in Likert scale are depicted in Fig. 4.
estimates.notes: MEASUREMENT-FORMAT VARIANT OF THE SAME THING, AND A USEFUL ONE FOR THE REVIEW: the identical population gives 68.2% on a yes/no item ('did you receive misinformation') and 75% on a Likert agree/strongly-agree item about having received inaccurate information - a seven-point gap driven purely by question format and by 'misinformation' versus 'inaccurate information' wording. Confidence medium because only the rounded 75% is given in the text; the exact item wording and the underlying counts live in Fig 4, which is an image, so no n is recoverable and the denominator (all 758, per 'of all respondents') is inferred from the text.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the professional subgroup breakdown of the headline exposure item - 'the prevalence was higher in the student's group (72.7% vs 65.7% in nonspecialist and 66.1% in the specialist group [p = 0.01])' - held back per the rule to keep the main figure rather than subgroup rows (note also that the text says there was 'no statistical difference in any group' and then reports p = 0.01, an internal contradiction the adjudicator should see); (2) sources of misinformation among those exposed - social media ranked first by 47.2% and family/friends second by 26.7%, and '70.02% of those who reported receiving inaccurate information named WhatsApp as the main source' - these are source attributions inside the exposed subgroup, not prevalence, and the 47.2% (social media) versus 70.02% (WhatsApp) figures sit oddly together; (3) the other Likert items, none of which measure encountering misinformation: information overload 67%, difficulty differentiating correct from incorrect information 50%, discomfort 26%, distraction from routine decision-making 33%, discomfort when not updated 50%, information helped contain COVID-19 72%, information should be regulated 74%; (4) rankings of formal and informal information SOURCES (government websites first for 63.1%, scientific journals first for 9.4%, online news first for 41.7% and second for 22.8%, social media first-or-second for 45.8%) - information diet, not misinformation; (5) the 24.8% of tweets containing misinformation and 17.4% unverified from Kouzy et al., the 32.5-81.3% guideline-adherence range from Hernandez-Garcia et al., the 110 internet sources of Cuan-Baltazar et al. and the 4.5% of H1N1 tweets from Chew & Eysenbach - all figures this paper cites from other studies, excluded by R8. Figures 1-4 are images, so no additional numbers can be read off them.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, 24 March - 10 April 2020, of healthcare personnel in India. Sampling frame: snowball sampling through an online Google Form circulated among medical students and physicians; email ID used as unique identifier to prevent duplicate submissions; submission taken as consent; institutional ethics committee approval obtained. 778 forms received, 20 incomplete, 758 analysed. A response rate cannot be computed for a snowball online survey (no defined denominator of invitees). Target sample size was 384 (assuming 42.2% misinformed, 5% absolute precision, 95% CI) and was exceeded. Instrument: developed after literature search and expert consultation (epidemiologists, medical educationists), cognitively pretested with 30 respondents using think-aloud, then pilot-tested on 50 more and revised. Analysis: chi-square tests, Stata 13. Measurement is entirely self-report with no verification of what respondents counted as misinformation; the authors list this as a limitation along with restriction to a literate, internet-connected population and snowball sampling bias.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation refers to false information which is shared without any intention of causing harm, while disinformation is fake information which has been deliberately created and shared to cause harm. The present study limits itself to misinformation only.
rob.item10_quote: Of all, 68.2% (95% CI: 64.8%e71.5%) respondents gave answers in affirmative for receiving misinformation. ... A total of 517 (68.2%) participants accepted receiving misinformation.
